blocks.text: India has six major physiographic divisions: the Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands.
They differ in geological origin, elevation, relief and landscape.

sections.title: Peninsular Plateau, desert, coasts and islands

blocks.text: The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient stable tableland, including the Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau. The Western Ghats are generally higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats.
The Indian Desert lies west of the Aravallis. Coastal Plains border the peninsula; Lakshadweep is mainly coral in origin and Andaman and Nicobar form an island chain.

revision.summary: India has six major physiographic divisions: the Himalayas, Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains and Islands. They differ in geological origin, elevation, relief and landscape. The Himalayas are young fold mountains arranged in parallel ranges. The Himadri is the highest northern range; the Himachal lies to its south; the Shiwaliks form the outermost range. The eastern hills beyond the Dihang gorge are collectively called the Purvachal. The Northern Plains were formed by alluvial deposits of the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries. They include the Punjab, Ganga and Brahmaputra plains. Bhabar is a pebbly belt near the Shiwaliks; Terai is marshy. Bhangar is older alluvium, while Khadar is newer alluvium. The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient stable tableland, including the Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau. The Western Ghats are generally higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats. The Indian Desert lies west of the Aravallis. Coastal Plains border the peninsula; Lakshadweep is mainly coral in origin and Andaman and Nicobar form an island chain.
